intro: Himi maps two trees, neither near the other. Oidani no Otsubaki, Japan's largest known wild camellia, sits in a remote hillside graveyard eighteen kilometres from the city centre; Jonichiji no Icho, one of the largest female ginkgos in the country, stands twenty minutes' walk from Himi Station. Published together under the 2026-08-31 exception: each is the reason to make the trip on its own, not a pair that adds up to a walk.
meta_description: Himi, Japan: Japan's largest wild camellia in a remote graveyard, and a 12-metre ginkgo at Jonichiji Temple near Himi Station.
question_meta: Himi's oldest tree is Jonichiji no Icho, a ginkgo of over a thousand years near Himi Station; its largest is the camellia Oidani no Otsubaki.
question_answer: Himi maps two trees. Jonichiji no Icho, a National Natural Monument ginkgo at Jonichiji Temple twenty minutes' walk from Himi Station, is the oldest, at over a thousand years by tradition. Oidani no Otsubaki, ranked Japan's largest known specimen of wild Camellia japonica, stands in a small community graveyard at the end of the remote Oidani valley, eighteen kilometres out.
question_context:
Jonichiji no Icho stands in the grounds of Jonichiji, a working Koyasan Shingon temple next to Asahiyama Park, an easy walk from the station. It became a National Natural Monument in 1926, one of the first trees in Japan ever given the designation, and local tradition credits the monk Hodo Shonin with planting it at the temple's founding in 681; taken literally that would make it over 1,300 years old, and the legend is usually rounded down to over a thousand instead. It is a female tree and a large one, roughly twelve metres round, said to be the largest female ginkgo in Japan by girth. Most autumns it drops around 180 litres of nuts, and mid-November is when its colour peaks.

Oidani no Otsubaki is a different visit: the far end of a dead-end valley, an ordinary open village graveyard, three trunks grown back together into a tangle solid enough to sit on. From the station that is a 35-minute taxi, or a bus to Shimo-Iwase plus a 30-minute walk. Budget a separate trip for each tree.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Himi?
faq.a: Jonichiji no Icho, a ginkgo at Jonichiji Temple said to be over a thousand years old, a National Natural Monument since 1926.

By girth, Jonichiji no Icho, roughly twelve metres round and said to be the largest female ginkgo in Japan. Oidani no Otsubaki, at 3.89 metres round, is separately ranked Japan's largest known wild camellia.

faq.q: Are the two trees near each other?
faq.a: No. They stand about 11 kilometres apart in different parts of Himi City and are best visited as two separate trips rather than one walk.
Yes, both trees stand on open ground with no ticket or booking.
Jonichiji no Icho is about 20 minutes on foot from Himi Station. Oidani no Otsubaki needs a 35-minute taxi from the station, or a bus to Shimo-Iwase plus a 30-minute walk.

trees.story:
Japan's thickest wild camellia stands in a village burial ground at the end of a dead-end valley. The Oidani camellia is ordinary yabu-tsubaki, Camellia japonica as it grows in the hills without anyone's help, and the surveyor Miyake Kazuyoshi ranked it first in the country for the species. It measures 3.89 metres round and 7.5 metres tall, spreading 7.9 metres east to west and 11 north to south.

Its age is disputed and we are not going to settle it. Himi City's own cultural-properties page says about 500 years. A 1998 published survey of Japan's giant trees says 700 to 800 instead. Neither explains how it got to its number.

The shape is what people come up here for. It splits into three thick trunks less than a metre off the ground, and their branches have grown back into each other into a tangle solid enough at around two and a half metres up to sit on. Locally it is the Sasumata Camellia, after the Y-shaped pole once used to pin a man against a wall.

The graveyard has a story attached. A samurai of Ikeda Castle executed on a false charge; his widow turned away by her own family and dead of grief; the two buried on the hill facing the castle, with a camellia planted where a stone should have gone. Toyama Prefecture designated the tree in 1965. It opens deep red for about a month from early April.

trees.access: Free, within the grounds of Jonichiji Temple, a functioning Koyasan Shingon Buddhist temple next to Asahiyama Park. National Natural Monument since 20 October 1926, so the grounds are a maintained public/visitable site; no entry fee or restriction found.
trees.transport: About 20 minutes on foot from Himi Station (JR West Himi Line).
trees.story:
Most autumns this ginkgo drops around 180 litres of nuts. It is a female tree, said to be the largest female ginkgo in Japan by girth and the largest ginkgo of any sex in Toyama: roughly 12 metres round and 24 metres tall, standing in the grounds of Jonichiji, a Koyasan Shingon temple twenty minutes on foot from Himi station.

It became a National Natural Monument on 20 October 1926, which puts it among the first trees in Japan ever given one. Local tradition holds that the itinerant monk Hodo Shonin planted it in 681, at the temple's founding, as a sacred tree. Taken literally that would make it 1,345 years old; the sources that repeat the legend all round it down to over 1,000 years, and the rounder figure is the honest one. The temple has been nicknamed Ginnan Shoja, the ginkgo hall, for centuries, after the tree rather than the other way round.

A folk remedy attached itself as well: the growths hanging from its limbs were shaved and brewed by women short of breast milk.

It is in good health. A local paper came to see it on 13 November 2025 and found it at the peak of its colour, which is also the week to go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 12 metres round, carrying a crown 24 metres up; nothing else on the site comes close to that size. It stands in the grounds of Jonichiji temple, beside Asahiyama Park.

best_time.label: mid November, when the ginkgo turns gold
